item.title: Rabobank profit flat as it braces for loan losses
item.description:
Rabobank profit flat as it braces for loan losses

August 4, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Rabobank made no profit growth in the first half of this year, reporting a net profit of nearly €2.7 billion, the same as in the first six months of 2025, after setting aside €562 million for loans that might not be repaid.

That is more than four times the €136 million it set aside a year earlier, the bank said in its results statement.

Chairman Stefaan Decraene told reporters the provisions related to two cases in South America but declined to name the companies or projects involved, broadcaster NOS reported.

Business in the Netherlands grew. Deposits at the Dutch retail arm stood at €375.1 billion, and lending at €293 billion.

Takeover talk
Decraene said Rabobank was open to buying another bank, telling NOS that scale is becoming more important.

Rabobank also said it will invest up to €2 billion in strengthening its data and IT systems and scaling up its use of artificial intelligence. Reuters reported that the spending will be spread over the next three years.

The bank’s return on equity was 9.5% and its core capital ratio 20.2%, which it said makes it one of the best-capitalised banks in Europe.

item.title: Man who held prison staff hostage given suspended jail sentence
item.description:
Man who held prison staff hostage given suspended jail sentence

August 4, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A man who held three prison staff hostage at knifepoint for several hours has been given a further suspended sentence of a year.

Corné H. seized and handcuffed his victims for several hours on December 5 last year at the jail in Vught after threatening them and five other colleagues with kitchen knives.

The 30-year-old had served a nine-month term for holding four staff at a bar in Ede, Gelderland, against their will in March the previous year.

At the time of the incident he was being detained in Vught’s psychiatric unit waiting to be given a place in a clinic under the Dutch compulsory treatment system (tbs).

The sentence was suspended to allow H. to continue his treatment, which began in June, meaning he will only have to go back to prison if he commits another offence.

The court in Den Bosch heard that H. suffered as a result of conditions including PTSS, schizophrenia and autism, which influenced his behaviour. A psychiatric assessment also said he had “anti-social and borderline personality traits”.

The judge said his victims feared for their lives and the incident “must have been dreadful for them”, but accepted H. had diminished responsibility and imposed a sentence that met the prosecution service’s demands.

At the earlier trial, H. was cleared of taking the bar staff in Ede hostage but convicted of depriving them of their liberty and threatening them.

Police sealed off the venue after he went in at closing time with guns and explosives and threatened to blow up the building, leading to a stand-off lasting more than eight hours.

item.title: Police raise concerns over sharp rise in weapon seizures
item.description:
Police raise concerns over sharp rise in weapon seizures

August 4, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dutch police seized 5,165 gas and alarm pistols, air weapons and pepper sprays last year, up from 4,080 in 2022, according to figures given to broadcaster NOS – a rise of almost 27%.

Police said they did not know whether the increase indicates that more people are carrying such weapons, or if it reflects boosted efforts to find and confiscate them.

Gas and alarm pistols are the main worry because they are hard to tell apart from real firearms, police spokesman Martin van der Meij told NOS. Alarm pistols make a loud bang but fire no projectile, while gas weapons can release tear gas.

They are cheap, easy to obtain and relatively simple to convert into working firearms, he said. A converted pistol was used to kill the crime reporter Peter R. de Vries in 2021.

Buying these weapons in Germany or Belgium and bringing them into the Netherlands is a criminal offence, though people do not always realise it.

Herman Oldenkotte, who runs a gun shop in Gronau just over the German border from Enschede, told NOS that he estimated 80% to 90% of his customers were Dutch. In Germany the weapons can be bought without a licence by anyone over 18.

Police also say more weapons are arriving by post. The Netherlands has pressed the EU for years to bring in a licence requirement or a ban.

Pepper spray is banned for civilians under Dutch weapons law. The justice ministry said in June it planned to allow permits for people at particular risk, such as stalking victims, while ruling out legalising it for everyone.

item.title: Limburg wildfire spreads across 100 hectares overnight
item.description:
Limburg wildfire spreads across 100 hectares overnight

August 4, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The wildfire in the Boschhuizerbergen nature reserve in northern Limburg has burned through about 100 hectares overnight and is still not under control, according to authorities, who have issued an NL-Alert warning to the surrounding area.

The Limburg-Noord emergency services authority (VRLN) said the fire had spread rapidly since Monday afternoon, when the area affected was 21 hectares, broadcaster NOS reported.

A spokesperson for the VRLN said on Tuesday morning that the fire had grown further overnight but was no longer spreading. Around 300 firefighters and emergency workers are tackling it, with crews sent from across the country.

Parts of the burned area have been put out, but the fire is still going elsewhere. Authorities have not yet said when it can be fully extinguished, saying it depends on conditions.

Two military helicopters dropped water over the site on Monday but had to stop at nightfall and are due to resume on Tuesday morning.

The NL-Alert warned that people should stay out of the smoke and close windows, doors and ventilation.

That alert remains in force, and NOS reported that a new one covering a wider area was expected on Tuesday morning because the wind has shifted.

A camping site, De Oude Barrier, has been evacuated and guests taken to a nearby hotel. Drones have also been banned from the area.

No trains are running between Boxmeer and Venray. Rail network operator ProRail expects the line to stay shut until at least 6pm on Tuesday.

The fire spread quickly because the wind strengthened and temperatures were high. The Netherlands is in an official water shortage after weeks with little rain.

item.description:
Police clear neighbourhood after explosives found in garden

August 4, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Bomb disposal specialists were called to a house in Rotterdam on Monday evening after a device was found during a police search.

Officers responded to reports of a person with a gun at the house in Voorne, in the Feijenoord district.

No weapons were found, but police cordoned off the area after explosives were found in the garden.

The disposal service EOD took the item away and destroyed it safely in the Kralingse Bos, Rotterdam’s largest urban park.

Police did not give any details of what the device was. Investigations are continuing.

item.title: Shell sells Dutch solar farms in retreat from renewables
item.description:
Shell sells Dutch solar farms in retreat from renewables

August 3, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Shell is selling every solar farm it owns in the Netherlands. The five sites, plus a combined wind and solar park at Pottendijk near Emmen, are going to the French oil company TotalEnergies.

The deal covers all of Shell’s wind and solar projects on land across Europe (its offshore windfarms are not included) and the company will not disclose what it is being paid.

The Dutch sites can produce up to 254 megawatts between them, enough to power tens of thousands of homes. They are at Moerdijk, Heerenveen, Emmen, and Sas van Gent and Koegorspolder near Terneuzen.

Some were built on land Shell had already used for oil and gas, and the company used them as proof it was changing. The Emmen farm stands on the site of an old gas treatment plant, part of a project Shell said could be an example for the rest of the country.

The sale needs approval from regulators and is expected to be completed at the end of 2026.

Retreating from transition
Wael Sawan, Shell’s chief executive, has shifted spending back towards oil and gas and away from low-carbon projects. TotalEnergies has moved the other way, buying renewable assets across Europe.

The Hague district court ordered Shell in 2021 to cut its emissions by 45% by 2030. The company dropped Royal Dutch from its name and moved its headquarters to London the following year, and won its appeal in November 2024.

Milieudefensie has taken that case to the Supreme Court and launched a second action last year over the company’s 700 oil and gas projects that are still in development.

Shell is not leaving Dutch renewable energy altogether. It keeps its stakes in North Sea wind farms, its Holland Hydrogen 1 plant at Rotterdam and its carbon capture work.

item.title: Doctors want more hospitals to offer late-term abortions
item.description:
Doctors want more hospitals to offer late-term abortions

August 3, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch association of gynaecologists, the NVOG, and the healthcare inspectorate IGJ want more hospitals to carry out late-term abortions – between 22 and 24 weeks – saying access to the care is not currently assured for all women.

Abortion is legal in the Netherlands up to 24 weeks. Terminations up to 22 weeks usually take place in abortion clinics, while those between 22 and 24 weeks are carried out in hospitals, of which only a small number currently do so.

Sanne Gordijn, head of obstetrics at the UMCG in Groningen, one of the few hospitals already providing the care, said some women were travelling to Spain, Britain or parts of the United States because they could not get a termination here.

She told broadcaster NOS that a late abortion is emotionally difficult for staff and never becomes routine, which is why the work needs to be shared out. The risk of medical complications after 22 weeks is why the procedure takes place in hospital.

Amsterdam’s OLVG has said it has been asked to take part but that reports it has already begun doing so are incorrect.

Gordijn said the grounds for a termination are usually a combination of factors, that the pregnant woman’s need comes first, and that no distinction is made between medical and non-medical grounds.

The UMCG said staff and medical social workers discuss the situation with women, including alternatives such as adoption, and that psychological support is available. Just over 39,000 abortions were carried out in the Netherlands in 2024, of which 331 were between 22 and 24 weeks.

Abortion clinics have reported a rise in attacks and intimidation in recent years, and MPs voted last year to bring forward a review of the abortion law, on a motion from NSC and the ChristenUnie.

item.title: Three terror suspects kept in custody as inquiries continue
item.description:
Three terror suspects kept in custody as inquiries continue

August 3, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Three teenagers who were arrested in dawn raids last week on suspicion of planning terrorist attacks have had their detention extended while police inquiries continue.

A 19-year-old man named as Muhammad K. was detained at his home in Eindhoven last Wednesday, at the same time as a 16-year-old youth from Rotterdam and a 17-year-old from De Rijp, a village near Alkmaar.

K. was sentenced to 112 days in prison and banned from travelling out of the Netherlands two years ago after a court convicted him of plotting attacks on nightclubs and police stations in Belgium. No attacks actually took place.

The other two suspects were among a group of 14 people aged between 14 and 30 who were arrested in April last year for allegedly inciting others to carry out terrorist attacks, using the social media platform TikTok.

The public prosecution service said the arrests were carried out by the special interventions service (DSI), acting on information from the intelligence agency AIVD. It added that no weapons were found during the raids and there were no signs that a specific attack was being planned or a target had been identified.

A magistrate in Rotterdam agreed last Friday to detain the trio in custody for a further 14 days.

item.title: PostNL delivers fewer parcels as Asian web orders decline
item.description:
PostNL delivers fewer parcels as Asian web orders decline

August 3, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch postal service PostNL delivered fewer letters and parcels in the first six months of this year, mainly due to a slump in orders from websites based in Asia.

The number of packages from abroad declined by 15% compared to the first half of 2025, the company’s latest quarterly figures show.

PostNL’s domestic deliveries declined in volume by 4.2%, reflecting the fact that consumers placed fewer orders. The total number of letters and cards sent was down by 8%, continuing a long-term trend.

However, PostNL’s turnover in the first six months was almost identical – €1,589 million, €1 million less than in 2025 – as the average cost per delivery increased by 4%.

Three-day deliveries

The trend is likely to continue as PostNL began imposing a €3 surcharge for all packages sent from outside the EU from July 1.

PostNL is also likely to benefit from a change in the law ending its obligation to deliver post within 24 hours. PostNL’s maximum delivery window was extended to two days on July 12 and will become three days next year, allowing it to charge extra for next-day deliveries.

CEO Pim Berendsen said he was satisfied with the results, but PostNL still needed to push through major reforms such as three-day deliveries to secure its future.

“Thanks to the disciplined rollout of our new strategy, we have achieved robust results and seen a strong improvement in our cashflow. At the sale time, we see external challenges are on the rise.”

item.title: Jumbo’s quinoa now comes from Groningen, not Peru
item.description:
Jumbo’s quinoa now comes from Groningen, not Peru

August 3, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

More than two dozen farmers in the Netherlands are growing quinoa, a South American seed that copes with salt far better than the crops usually planted on coastal land.

Salt is a worsening problem around the Dutch coast, with too little fresh water flowing to hold back the sea, and salt also seeps up from the ground in dry conditions.

This destroys potato and onion yields, but quinoa can survive much more easily, being able to withstand up to 12 grams of salt per litre of water. Potatoes begin to struggle at one gram.

Robert Van Loom, a researcher at Wageningen University, began breeding quinoa for Dutch conditions in the 1990s. He crossed an Ecuadorian variety, which could not handle the long Dutch summer days, with a Chilean one that was too bitter to sell. That cross became the basis for growing quinoa across Europe.

Renze Rispens, a farmer in Vierhuizen in Groningen, grows crops close to the sea dyke, on ground that has always carried a lot of salt. He read about quinoa in a trade magazine and planted it last year. Even in this summer’s drought, he said, the crop is standing well.

Most growers have contracts with GreenFood50, set up to sell Dutch-grown quinoa. Founder Marc Arts said its farmers now work about 200 hectares, producing 600 tonnes a year. A few others grow it independently.

Jumbo has switched its own-brand quinoa entirely to organic Dutch supply, under a three-year contract covering 12 farmers. Dutch quinoa costs more to buy in than imported, sustainability manager Marjolein Verkerk said, but she expects that to level out. The chain sells hundreds of thousands of packs a year.

Quinoa grew up around Lake Titicaca in the Andes, which was once a saltwater lake. That is where the salt tolerance comes from.
